analogy.p: Think of the cell as a pump, the current as the flow of water and the p.d. as the pressure the pump gives. In a series circuit there is one pipe with several narrow sections: the same flow of water passes through each part, and the pressure drop is shared between the narrow sections. In a parallel circuit the pipe splits into two side pipes: both side pipes have the same pressure difference across them, but the flow splits, with more water going down the wider pipe. The analogy breaks down because water pressure can be lost to leaks and friction in more ways than in wires, and real electrons carry no mass flow that you could see.

bullets: **Series**: one loop, one path; if one component breaks the whole circuit stops.
**Parallel**: separate branches joined at **junctions**; if one branch breaks, the others still work.
A **junction** is a point where wires join and the current divides or recombines.
Use **circuit symbols** for cell, battery, switch, resistor, lamp, ammeter and voltmeter in diagrams.
The **cell or battery** gives the circuit its potential difference; several cells in series add their p.d.
Ammeters go **in series**; voltmeters go **in parallel** across a component.
Household lights and sockets are wired **in parallel** so each can be switched independently and gets the full mains p.d.
core.h: Series and parallel: the two ways to connect components
core.p: Components can be connected in a **series circuit**, where they are joined end to end in a single loop so that there is only **one path** for charge to flow, or in a **parallel circuit**, where the circuit splits into **separate branches** and the charge has more than one path. Most real circuits, including those in houses, contain both. Being able to look at a diagram and say which components are in series with which, and which are in parallel, is the first skill. Components are **in series** if the same current must pass through each one; they are **in parallel** if each is connected across the same two points.

bullets: **I is the same everywhere**: I (cell) = I1 = I2 = I3.
Reason: **charge is conserved**; electrons are not used up as they go round.
The ammeter reading is unchanged by moving the ammeter to a different place in the loop.
Current is found from **I = V / R** using the total p.d. and total resistance.
Adding more components in series **reduces** the current (because total resistance increases).
If a bulb in a series circuit blows, the current drops to **zero** because the loop is broken.
Example: a 6 V cell and resistors of 2 ohms and 4 ohms: current = 6 / 6 = **1 A** through both.
core.p: In a **series circuit the current is the same at every point**. Charge cannot build up or vanish anywhere in the loop, so the **rate of flow of charge** must be identical through every component and through the cell. This is why an ammeter placed anywhere in a series loop gives the same reading. It does not matter if the components have different resistances: the larger resistance simply takes a larger share of the p.d. rather than reducing the current in one place only. The size of the current for the whole circuit depends on the **total resistance** and the **cell p.d.**

bullets: **V (supply) = V1 + V2 + V3** for components in series.
V across each component = **I x R** using the common current.
The **larger resistor** has the **larger p.d.** across it.
In the example (6 V, 2 ohms, 4 ohms, 1 A): **V1 = 1 x 2 = 2 V** and **V2 = 1 x 4 = 4 V**, which sum to 6 V.
**Cells in series** add their p.d.: two 1.5 V cells give 3.0 V.
A voltmeter across **two** components in series reads the sum of their p.d.s.
This is the idea behind a **potential divider**: the p.d. splits in proportion to the resistances.
core.p: In a **series circuit the total potential difference of the supply is shared between the components**. The p.d. is the energy transferred per unit charge, so the energy each coulomb of charge picks up from the cell is transferred to the components it passes through on the way round. The p.d. across each component is found from **V = I R**, so the component with the **greater resistance takes the greater share** of the supply p.d. The p.d.s across the components add up to the p.d. of the supply.

bullets: **R total = R1 + R2 + R3 (ohms)**.
Total resistance **increases** every time a resistor is added in series.
R total is **greater than** the biggest individual resistor.
In terms of the electrons: they must make their way through **each resistor in turn**, colliding with ions in each one.
Use R total with the cell p.d. in **I = V / R** to find the overall current.
Components with greater resistance in series transfer more energy per second (P = I squared R, with the same I).
Two 4 ohm resistors in series have a total resistance of **8 ohms**.
core.p: The **total resistance of components in series is the sum of the individual resistances**: **R total = R1 + R2 + R3**. Adding another resistor in series makes the path harder for the charge to flow through, because the charge has to pass through every resistor in turn. So the **total resistance is always greater than the largest single resistance**. This is also why adding more bulbs in series makes each bulb dimmer: the current falls, so each bulb transfers less energy per second.

bullets: **I total = I1 + I2 + I3** (branch currents).
At a junction: **current in = current out** (charge is conserved).
A **branch with lower resistance** has **more current** than one with higher resistance.
Each branch behaves independently: changing one branch does not change the current in the others.
An ammeter in the main wire reads the **total** current; one in a branch reads only that branch.
Adding another branch **increases the total current** drawn from the supply.
Example: 12 V across 6 ohm and 3 ohm branches gives **2 A** and **4 A**, total **6 A**.
core.p: In a **parallel circuit the current from the supply splits at a junction** and the currents in the branches add up to the total current. The **total current drawn from the cell is the sum of the currents through each branch**. This follows from **conservation of charge**: charge arriving at a junction must leave it, so the total current into the junction equals the total current out. The branch with the **smaller resistance** carries the **larger current**, because the p.d. across each branch is the same and I = V / R.

bullets: **V is the same across every parallel branch**: V (supply) = V1 = V2 = V3.
Reason: each branch is connected across the **same two points**.
In the example every branch has **12 V** across it.
Parallel cells have the **same p.d.** as one cell but can supply current for longer.
Use **V = I R** with the branch p.d. and the branch resistance to find each branch current.
If one branch is broken, the p.d. across the others stays the same.
Domestic circuits being parallel is why **each appliance works at full mains p.d.**
core.p: In a **parallel circuit the potential difference across each branch is the same as the p.d. of the supply**. Each branch is connected directly across the same two points of the cell, so each coulomb of charge that goes through any branch transfers the same amount of energy. This is why lamps connected in parallel are as bright as a single lamp connected to the same cell, and why household appliances are connected in parallel: each gets the full **230 V mains** p.d. A voltmeter placed across any branch reads the supply p.d. (if the cell has negligible internal resistance).

bullets: **R total < the smallest resistor** in parallel.
More branches means **more paths**, so **more total current** for the same p.d.
Larger total current at the same p.d. means **lower total resistance** (R = V / I).
Extension (not required by AQA): **1 / R total = 1 / R1 + 1 / R2**.
For **two equal resistors R** in parallel the total is **R / 2**.
A 6 ohm and 3 ohm resistor in parallel give a total of **2 ohms**: check **12 V / 6 A = 2 ohms**.
Total resistance can be found without a formula using **R = V (supply) / I (total)**.
core.p: When resistors are connected in **parallel the total resistance is less than the resistance of the smallest individual resistor**. Adding another branch gives the charge **another path** to flow along, so for the same p.d. a **greater total current** flows from the cell. Since R = V / I, a larger total current for the same p.d. means a smaller total resistance. It is like opening extra tills in a supermarket: more people (charge) can get through in the same time. This is a **Higher tier** idea in AQA, and you must be able to explain it in words even though the formula is not required.

bullets: **Series**: I same, V shared (V total = V1 + V2), R total = R1 + R2.
**Parallel**: V same, I shared (I total = I1 + I2), R total smaller than smallest R.
**Quick memory**: series = same current, shared p.d.; parallel = same p.d., shared current.
Adding a component in series: **I falls**, R total rises.
Adding a branch in parallel: **I total rises**, R total falls.
The **same equation V = I R** applies to each component and to the whole circuit.
core.h: Comparing series and parallel in a table of rules
core.p: The cleanest way to revise is to compare the two types side by side for each quantity. Remember that current and p.d. behave in opposite ways: in **series the current is the same and the p.d. is shared**, whereas in **parallel the p.d. is the same and the current is shared**. Total resistance also behaves oppositely: it **increases** when a resistor is added in series and **decreases** when one is added in parallel. Questions often ask you to apply these rules to a circuit with an ammeter or voltmeter and fill in the missing values.

bullets: **Set-up**: cell or power supply, switch, the resistor (or combination) under test, an **ammeter in series** and a **voltmeter in parallel** across only the test part.
**Method**: close the switch, record the ammeter current I and voltmeter p.d. V, then work out **R = V / I**; repeat for a single resistor, two in series, and two in parallel.
**Expected pattern**: the series pair gives a **larger** R than either resistor; the parallel pair gives a **smaller** R than either resistor.
**Several readings**: change the p.d. (variable supply or variable resistor) to get a range of V and I, then take a **mean R** or the gradient of a V-I graph.
**Control variables**: keep the same wire or resistors, a **low p.d.**, and **switch off between readings** so the wire does not heat up and change its resistance.
**Risks and controls**: wires and resistors can get hot at higher current (keep p.d. low, switch off between readings, let them cool); do not touch bare connections.
**Zero error**: check meters read zero before connecting; reading the scale at eye level and to a sensible number of significant figures improves accuracy.
**Evaluate**: compare measured R with the calculated series or parallel value, give a percentage difference, and comment on contact resistance and meter precision.
core.h: Required practical 15: investigating resistance with circuit diagrams
core.p: The AQA required practical asks you to use **circuit diagrams to set up and check circuits** that investigate the factors affecting resistance, including **combinations of resistors in series and in parallel** (and the length of a wire at constant temperature). The idea is to measure the **p.d. across** and the **current through** a resistor or combination, calculate **R = V / I**, and compare your result with the value predicted by the series and parallel rules. Because you are checking a rule, accuracy and careful meter placement matter: the ammeter must be in series and the voltmeter must be in parallel with the part being tested, or the readings are meaningless.

bullets: **Step 1**: R total = R1 + R2 + ...
**Step 2**: I = V supply / R total.
**Step 3**: V1 = I x R1, V2 = I x R2 and so on.
**Step 4**: check **V1 + V2 = V supply**.
Rearrangements: **R = V / I**, **V = I R**, **I = V / R**.
Show units: volts (V), amps (A), ohms (ohm).
Be careful with **milliamps**: divide by 1000 to convert to amps.
core.p: A reliable method is to work in the same order every time. First find the **total resistance** by adding. Then find the **current** using the cell p.d. and the total resistance (**I = V / R**). Then use that current for every component, calculating each p.d. with **V = I R**, and check that the p.d.s add up to the cell p.d. Write the equation, substitute values with units and give the final answer with the correct unit. Always check that your answer makes sense: the p.d.s must add up to the supply p.d.

bullets: Parallel branch current: **I = V / R** with V being the branch (= supply) p.d.
Total current: **I total = I1 + I2**.
Total resistance of the parallel part: **R = V / I total** (or the extension formula).
Combined circuit: R total = series resistor + resistance of the parallel part.
Find the p.d. across the series resistor with V = I R; the **parallel part gets the remaining p.d.**
Example: 12 V, a 4 ohm resistor in series with 6 ohm and 12 ohm in parallel: **I total = 1.5 A**, **6 V** across the 4 ohm resistor, **6 V** across each parallel branch.
Check that the **parallel branch currents add to the total current**.
core.h: Calculating in parallel and combined circuits
core.p: For a parallel circuit, start with the **branch p.d.**, which equals the supply p.d., then find the current in each branch with **I = V / R** and add them to get the total current. For a **combined circuit** (a series part and a parallel part) find the total resistance of the parallel part first, treat it as a single resistor in series with the rest, then work back to find the p.d. across each part. This **Higher-tier** approach needs care, so set it out in clear steps and check the totals at the end.

bullets: **Mains sockets are in parallel** so that each appliance gets the full 230 V and can be switched independently.
Fuses and switches are placed in the **live wire**, in series with the appliance.
In series, power transferred in each component is **P = I squared R**; in parallel, **P = V squared / R**.
The total power of a parallel circuit is the **sum of the powers of the branches**.
**Thermistors and LDRs** in series with a resistor form a potential divider in sensor circuits.
Ammeters have low resistance and are in series; voltmeters have high resistance and are in parallel.
Link to **I-V characteristics**: components in series or parallel each keep their own characteristic.
core.h: Links to other topics and everyday applications
core.p: Series and parallel rules are used throughout Physics. They explain how **household circuits** are wired (parallel), why **Christmas lights** in old series strings all went out when one blew, and how **sensor circuits** use potential dividers. They link to **power (P = I V)**: in parallel branches the one with the lower resistance transfers energy faster, and the total power is the sum of the branch powers. They also underpin the **National Grid**, where transformers keep current low to reduce energy loss, and the later electromagnetism topics.

exam: **State/identify** (1 mark): 'the current is the same in a series circuit'; 'the p.d. is the same across each branch in parallel'.
**Calculate** (2 to 3 marks): write the equation (R total = R1 + R2, V = I R), substitute, give the answer with units; marks for the correct method even if the arithmetic is wrong.
**Explain** why adding a resistor in series increases the total resistance (2 marks): charge has to pass through every resistor in turn, so the total opposition is greater.

**Explain** (Higher tier) why adding a resistor in parallel decreases the total resistance (3 marks): another path for charge, so more current flows from the supply for the same p.d., so lower resistance.
**Circuit with ammeters and voltmeters** (3 to 4 marks): apply series and parallel rules to fill in missing readings, showing steps.
**Combined circuit** (4 to 6 marks): find the parallel resistance first, add the series resistor, find the total current, then the p.d.s and branch currents.
**Compare** (2 to 4 marks): use a parallel structure: 'In series ...; in parallel ...' for current, p.d. and resistance.
**Why are homes wired in parallel?** (2 marks): each appliance gets the full mains p.d. and can be switched on and off independently.
**Check answers**: p.d.s in series must add to the supply; branch currents must add to the total current.
**Show working**: each correct stage of a calculation can earn a mark even if the final answer is wrong.
Use the **exact phrases** 'shared between', 'the same across', 'conservation of charge' and 'another path' in explanations.

mistakes.r: The p.d. is the same across each branch; the current splits and is larger in the branch with the smaller resistance.
mistakes.w: In a parallel circuit the current is the same in every branch.

mistakes.r: The current is the same; the p.d. of the supply is shared between the components.
mistakes.w: In a series circuit the p.d. is the same across every component.

mistakes.r: Adding a resistor in parallel decreases the total resistance because there is another path for the charge.
mistakes.w: Adding a resistor in parallel increases the total resistance.

mistakes.r: The total resistance of parallel resistors is smaller than the smallest, so find the total current and use R = V / I.
mistakes.w: Adding up the resistances in parallel to find the total.

mistakes.r: An ammeter must be placed in series; a voltmeter is placed in parallel.
mistakes.w: Putting the ammeter in parallel with the component.

mistakes.r: The current is the same all the way round a series loop; energy is transferred, not charge used up.
mistakes.w: The current gets used up as it passes through components.

mistakes.r: A voltmeter measures the potential difference; an ammeter measures current.
Give V in volts, I in amps and R in ohms.
mistakes.w: Forgetting units or writing V for resistance.

mistakes.r: The component in a series circuit has only part of the supply p.d.; use V = I R with the common current.
mistakes.w: Using the supply p.d. across a component in series.

summary: You must know the rules for current, potential difference and resistance in series and parallel circuits, use them to calculate unknown values (including Higher-tier combined circuits), and explain why adding resistors in series increases total resistance while adding them in parallel decreases it. It matters because these rules appear in nearly every circuits question and underpin domestic wiring and the National Grid.

terms.d: A circuit in which components are connected one after another in a single loop, with the same current through all components.
A circuit in which components are connected on separate branches, each connected across the same two points, so the p.d. across each is the same.
The rate of flow of electric charge, measured in amps.
The energy transferred per unit charge between two points in a circuit, measured in volts.
The opposition to the flow of charge in a component or circuit, measured in ohms, R = V / I.
The single resistance that could replace all of the components in a circuit and give the same current from the same p.d.
A point in a circuit where wires meet and the current divides or combines.
One of the separate paths in a parallel circuit.
A meter connected in series that measures the current in a circuit and has very low resistance.
A meter connected in parallel that measures the p.d. across a component and has very high resistance.
Charge is neither created nor destroyed, so the total current entering a junction equals the total current leaving it.
A device that supplies a potential difference using a chemical reaction; several cells connected in series form a battery.
For a component at constant temperature the current is directly proportional to the p.d. across it, V = I R.
The potential difference provided by the cell or power supply across the whole circuit.
The a.c. supply in the UK, about 230 V at 50 Hz, with household appliances connected in parallel.
A fault in a measuring instrument in which it reads a value other than zero when it should read zero, giving every reading the same error.
The AQA investigation using circuit diagrams to set up and check circuits for the factors affecting resistance, including resistors in series and in parallel.

worked.ans: R total = 6.0 ohms; I = 1.0 A; V1 = 2.0 V; V2 = 4.0 V.
worked.q: A 6.0 V cell is connected in series to a 2.0 ohm resistor and a 4.0 ohm resistor. Calculate the total resistance, the current and the p.d. across each resistor. (5 marks)
steps: The current is the same through both resistors in series.
Check: 2.0 + 4.0 = 6.0 V, equal to the cell p.d.

worked.ans: I1 = 2.0 A, I2 = 4.0 A, I total = 6.0 A, R total = 2.0 ohms.
worked.q: A 12 V supply is connected across a 6.0 ohm resistor and a 3.0 ohm resistor in parallel. Calculate the current in each branch, the total current and the total resistance. (5 marks)
steps: The p.d. across each branch is 12 V.
This is less than the smallest resistor (3.0 ohms), as expected.

worked.ans: Current from the battery = 1.5 A; p.d. across the parallel pair = 6.0 V (branch currents 1.0 A and 0.50 A).
worked.q: A 12 V battery is connected to a 4.0 ohm resistor in series with a parallel pair of 6.0 ohm and 12 ohm resistors. Calculate the current from the battery and the p.d. across the parallel pair. (6 marks, Higher tier)
steps: Find the resistance of the parallel pair: 1 / R = 1/6 + 1/12 = 3/12, so R = 4.0 ohms.
p.d. across the series 4.0 ohm resistor = 1.5 x 4.0 = 6.0 V.
p.d. across the parallel pair = 12 - 6.0 = 6.0 V.
Check branch currents: 6.0 / 6.0 = 1.0 A and 6.0 / 12 = 0.50 A, which add to 1.5 A.
